NASM Syntax & Directives: section .data  // initialized data section (constants, strings, arrays)
global _start  // make _start visible to linker (ELF entry point)
extern printf  // declare external symbol from C library
times 64 db 0  // repeat directive: reserve 64 zero bytes
$  // current address (used for string length: len equ $ - msg)
align 16  // align next instruction/data to 16-byte boundary
default rel  // use RIP-relative addressing by default
Registers: rax  // accumulator: syscall number, return value, arithmetic
rcx  // counter: loop count, shift amount (caller-saved)
rdx  // data register: 3rd syscall arg, multiply/divide (caller-saved)
rsi  // source index: 2nd syscall arg, string ops (caller-saved)
rdi  // destination index: 1st syscall arg, string ops (caller-saved)
rbp  // base pointer: stack frame reference (callee-saved)
rsp  // stack pointer: points to top of stack
r8-r15  // extended registers: r8 (5th arg), r9 (6th arg)
eax / ax / al  // 32/16/8-bit subregister of rax (zero-extends on write)
rflags  // status flags: CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF, IF, DF
rip  // instruction pointer (read-only, used for RIP-relative addr)
Instructions: mov rax, rbx  // copy rbx into rax (register to register)
mov rax, [rbx]  // load from memory at address in rbx
mov [rdi], rax  // store rax to memory at address in rdi
lea rbx, [rax+rcx*4]  // load effective address (no memory access)
add rax, rbx  // rax = rax + rbx
sub rax, rbx  // rax = rax - rbx
inc rax / dec rax  // increment/decrement by 1
mul rbx  // unsigned multiply: rdx:rax = rax * rbx
div rcx  // unsigned divide: rax=quotient, rdx=remainder
imul rax, rbx, 10  // signed multiply: rax = rbx * 10
xor rax, rbx  // bitwise XOR (xor same reg = zero idiom)
not rax  // bitwise NOT (flip all bits)
shl rax, cl  // shift left by cl bits (multiply by 2^cl)
shr rax, cl  // shift right by cl bits (unsigned divide by 2^cl)
sar rax, cl  // arithmetic shift right (preserves sign bit)
rol rax, cl  // rotate left through all bits
ror rax, cl  // rotate right through all bits
Control Flow: jmp label  // unconditional jump to label
je / jne  // jump if equal / not equal (ZF=1 / ZF=0)
jg / jl / jge / jle  // signed greater/less (SF, OF, ZF flags)
ja / jb / jae / jbe  // unsigned above/below (CF, ZF flags)
jo / js / jp / jc  // overflow, sign, parity, carry
cmp rax, rbx  // compare: sets flags (like sub without store)
test rax, rbx  // bitwise AND that sets flags (like and without store)
loop label  // dec rcx; jump if rcx != 0
call label  // push return address, jump to procedure
ret  // pop return address, jump back
cmovg rax, rbx  // conditional move: rax=rbx if greater (avoids branch)
sete al  // set byte to 1 if equal, else 0
Stack & Procedures: push rax  // decrement rsp by 8, store rax at [rsp]
pop rax  // load rax from [rsp], increment rsp by 8
push rbp  // save base pointer (prologue start)
mov rbp, rsp  // set stack frame base
sub rsp, 32  // allocate 32 bytes for local variables
leave  // restore rsp and pop rbp (shortcut for mov rsp,rbp; pop rbp)
syscall  // invoke Linux kernel: rax=syscall#, args in rdi,rsi,rdx,r10,r8,r9
extern printf  // call C library function (link with -lc)
global main  // entry point when using libc (gcc -no-pie link)
System Calls (Linux x64): mov rax, 0 ; sys_read  // read from file descriptor: rdi=fd, rsi=buf, rdx=count
mov rax, 1 ; sys_write  // write to fd: rdi=fd, rsi=buf, rdx=count
mov rax, 2 ; sys_open  // open file: rdi=path, rsi=flags, rdx=mode
mov rax, 3 ; sys_close  // close fd: rdi=fd
mov rax, 9 ; sys_mmap  // mmap: rdi=addr, rsi=len, rdx=prot, r10=flags, r8=fd, r9=off

backend.title: No Database Index
backend.desc: Query scans entire table due to missing index.
backend.bug:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT,
  total DECIMAL(10,2),
  status VARCHAR(20)
);
-- Query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123
-- No index on user_id → full table scan!
backend.solution:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT,
  total DECIMAL(10,2),
  status VARCHAR(20),
  INDEX idx_user_id (user_id)
);
-- Now the query uses the index!

FROM node:20
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN npm install
RUN npm run build
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
backend.solution:
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

backend.title: Inefficient Subquery vs JOIN
backend.desc: Correlated subquery executes once per row instead of JOIN.
backend.bug:
SELECT u.*,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id) as order_count,
  (SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id) as total_spent
FROM users u
WHERE u.created_at > '2024-01-01'
-- Runs 2 subqueries per user — O(n) queries!
backend.solution:
SELECT u.*,
  COUNT(o.id) as order_count,
  COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) as total_spent
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE u.created_at > '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY u.id
-- Single efficient query!

-- Down

-- Run with migration tool:
-- npm run migrate:up

  user_id INT,
  total DECIMAL(10,2),
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
  -- No index on user_id! JOINs scan full table
);
backend.solution:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT,
  total DECIMAL(10,2),
  INDEX idx_orders_user_id (user_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);

backend.title: Missing Composite Index
backend.desc: Query filtering by two columns needs a composite index.

backend.title: No Request Body Size Limit
backend.desc: Express JSON parser has no size limit.

backend.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference
backend.desc: API exposes internal IDs that can be enumerated.

backend.title: No Fallback for Downstream Service
backend.desc: Third-party API failure causes the whole endpoint to fail.

backend.title: No Vendor Prefix on CSS Cache
backend.desc: Static file serving missing immutable cache headers.
backend.bug:
app.use(express.static('public'));
// No cache headers — browser re-fetches every time!

backend.title: Missing Content Security Policy
backend.desc: No CSP header — vulnerable to XSS attacks.

backend.title: API Without Versioning
backend.desc: API has no version prefix — backward compatibility is impossible.

backend.title: Excessive Data Exposure
backend.desc: API returns the entire database row including sensitive fields.

backend.title: Slow COUNT Query on Large Table
backend.desc: COUNT(*) on InnoDB with no WHERE causes full index scan.

backend.title: No Connection Limit Per User
backend.desc: A single user can exhaust all database connections.
backend.bug:
-- No per-user connection limits
-- Any user can open 1000 connections and block others!

backend.title: Missing Query Timeout
backend.desc: Long-running queries hold database locks and connections.

backend.title: No Rate Limiting on Auth Endpoint
backend.desc: Login endpoint has no rate limiting — brute force possible.

backend.title: No Database Query Logging
backend.desc: Slow queries are not logged for debugging.

backend.title: No Database Query Plan Analysis
backend.desc: Missing EXPLAIN on queries to detect full table scans.

backend.title: Wrong Index Type for Range Query
backend.desc: Hash index used on column with range queries.
backend.solution:
CREATE INDEX idx_created_at ON orders USING BTREE (created_at);
-- BTREE supports range queries, sorting, and prefix matching!

backend.title: No Readiness Probe in K8s
backend.desc: Kubernetes doesn't know when the app is ready for traffic.
backend.bug:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        # No readiness probe — may send traffic before app is ready!
backend.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/ready
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/live
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20

backend.title: Missing Resource Limits in K8s
backend.desc: Container can consume all node resources.
backend.bug:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        # No resource limits — can OOM the node!
backend.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: '256Mi'
            cpu: '250m'
          limits:
            memory: '512Mi'
            cpu: '500m'

backend.title: No Liveness Probe in K8s
backend.desc: Hanging application never restarted by Kubernetes.
backend.bug:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        # No liveness probe — if app hangs, it stays dead!
backend.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/live
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
          failureThreshold: 3

backend.title: Secret Exposed in Environment
backend.desc: Kubernetes secret passed as plain env var can be read from /proc.
backend.bug:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          value: 'supersecret' # Visible in pod description!
backend.solution:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  password: c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQ=
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-secret
              key: password

backend.title: No Pre-stop Hook in K8s
backend.desc: Container is killed immediately without graceful drain.
backend.bug:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        # No preStop — connections are cut immediately!
backend.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ['/bin/sh', '-c', 'sleep 10']
        terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

backend.title: No Pod Anti-Affinity
backend.desc: Multiple replicas can be scheduled on the same node.
backend.bug:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      # No anti-affinity — all pods could land on one node!
      # Node failure takes down all replicas
backend.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 100
            podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  app: myapp
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

backend.title: No PDB for Critical Service
backend.desc: Voluntary node drains can kill all replicas simultaneously.
backend.bug:
# No PodDisruptionBudget — during node maintenance
# all pods can be evicted at once causing downtime!
backend.solution:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: app-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp

backend.title: Missing Graceful Shutdown Handler
backend.desc: Docker stop sends SIGTERM but app doesn't handle it.

backend.title: Wrong Content-Type for File Upload
backend.desc: File upload endpoint expects wrong content type.

backend.title: No Timezone Handling in Dates
backend.desc: Storing dates without timezone causes off-by-hour bugs.

backend.title: No Backup for Database
backend.desc: Production database has no automated backup.
backend.bug:
# No cron job for database backup
# If database corrupts, all data is lost forever!
backend.solution:
#!/bin/bash
# backup.sh — run daily via cron
BACKUP_DIR=/backups/$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
mkdir -p $BACKUP_DIR
pg_dump myapp > $BACKUP_DIR/db.sql
gzip $BACKUP_DIR/db.sql
aws s3 cp $BACKUP_DIR/db.sql.gz s3://myapp-backups/
# Delete backups older than 30 days
find /backups/* -mtime +30 -exec rm -rf {} \;

backend.title: No Monitoring for Critical Metrics
backend.desc: No monitoring means downtime goes undetected.
backend.bug:
# No monitoring setup
# Server could be down for hours without anyone knowing!

backend.title: No Rate Limit for File Upload
backend.desc: File uploads without rate limit can fill disk space.

backend.title: No Index on Date Column for Range Query
backend.desc: Date range queries without index scan full table.
backend.bug:
-- Query: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'
-- No index on created_at — full table scan!
backend.solution:
CREATE INDEX idx_logs_created_at ON logs(created_at);
-- Now range queries use index scan

backend.title: No Connection Encryption
backend.desc: Database connection without TLS — credentials sent in plaintext.

backend.title: Session Fixation Vulnerability
backend.desc: Server accepts pre-set session IDs from URL params.

backend.title: No HSTS Header
backend.desc: Missing HTTP Strict-Transport-Security header allows SSL stripping.

backend.title: No Audit Log for Admin Actions
backend.desc: Admin actions are not logged for security audit.

backend.title: No Health Check for Dependencies
backend.desc: Health endpoint doesn't check downstream services.

backend.title: No Forwarded IP Header
backend.desc: Reverse proxy doesn't forward original client IP.

backend.title: No WebSocket Authentication
backend.desc: WebSocket connections are not authenticated.

backend.title: No Backpressure Handling in Stream
backend.desc: Streaming response without backpressure causes OOM.

backend.title: No User-Agent Validation
backend.desc: API doesn't validate User-Agent header for bot detection.

backend.title: No Request Body Validation in Lambda
backend.desc: Serverless function doesn't validate event body structure.

backend.title: Cold Start Optimization Missing
backend.desc: Lambda function has large dependencies causing slow cold starts.

backend.title: No SQS Dead Letter Queue
backend.desc: Failed SQS messages are retried infinitely or discarded.
backend.bug:
Resources:
  MyQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      VisibilityTimeout: 30
      # No RedrivePolicy — failed messages lost forever after maxReceiveCount!
backend.solution:
Resources:
  MyQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      VisibilityTimeout: 30
      RedrivePolicy:
        deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt MyDLQ.Arn
        maxReceiveCount: 3

  MyDLQ:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600 # 14 days

backend.title: No Retry on DynamoDB Throttling
backend.desc: DynamoDB writes fail when exceeding provisioned throughput.

backend.title: No VPC Isolation for RDS
backend.desc: Database is exposed to the public internet.
backend.bug:
Resources:
  MyDB:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      PubliclyAccessible: true # Database accessible from internet!
      # No security group restriction!
backend.solution:
Resources:
  MyDB:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      PubliclyAccessible: false
      VPCSecurityGroups:
        - !Ref DatabaseSecurityGroup
      DBSubnetGroupName: !Ref MyDBSubnetGroup

  DatabaseSecurityGroup:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: Database access
      SecurityGroupIngress:
        - IpProtocol: tcp
          FromPort: 5432
          ToPort: 5432
          SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref AppSecurityGroup

backend.title: No S3 Bucket Versioning
backend.desc: S3 bucket has no versioning — accidental deletion is permanent.
backend.bug:
Resources:
  MyBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      # No VersioningConfiguration — deleted/overwritten files are gone forever!
backend.solution:
Resources:
  MyBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      LifecycleConfiguration:
        Rules:
          - Id: ExpireOldVersions
            Status: Enabled
            NoncurrentVersionExpirationInDays: 90

backend.title: No IAM Role for Lambda
backend.desc: Lambda function uses root credentials instead of IAM role.
backend.solution:
# Lambda execution role with least privilege
Resources:
  LambdaExecutionRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service: lambda.amazonaws.com
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: S3WriteAccess
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: s3:PutObject
                Resource: arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*

cs.title: Fix Main Signature
cs.desc: The Main method has an incorrect signature.
cs.bug:
using System;
class Program { static void main() { Console.WriteLine("Hi"); } }
cs.solution:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { Console.WriteLine("Hi"); } }

cs.title: Fix String Interpolation
cs.desc: The string interpolation syntax is wrong.
cs.bug:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { string name = "world"; Console.WriteLine("Hello {name}"); } }
cs.solution:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { string name = "world"; Console.WriteLine($"Hello {name}"); } }

cs.title: Fix Array Initialization
cs.desc: The array initialization syntax is incorrect.
cs.bug:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { int[] arr = new int[3] {1,2,3}; Console.WriteLine(arr[0]); } }
cs.solution:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { int[] arr = {1,2,3}; Console.WriteLine(arr[0]); } }

php.title: Fix PDO Query
php.desc: The PDO query is vulnerable to SQL injection.
php.bug:
<?php
$pdo = new PDO('sqlite::memory:');
$id = $_GET['id'];
$stmt = $pdo->query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $id");
?>
php.solution:
<?php
$pdo = new PDO('sqlite::memory:');
$id = $_GET['id'];
$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
$stmt->execute([$id]);
?>

php.title: Fix Class Constructor
php.desc: The class constructor uses old PHP 4 syntax.
php.bug:
<?php
class Person {
  var $name;
  function Person($name) {
    $this->name = $name;
  }
}
$p = new Person("Alice");
echo $p->name;
?>

<?php
class Person {
  public $name;
  function __construct($name) {
    $this->name = $name;

}

?>

php.title: Fix Type Hinting
php.desc: The scalar type hint is not strict.
php.bug:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
function add(int $a, int $b): int {
  return $a + $b;
}
echo add("5", 3);
?>
php.solution:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
function add(int $a, int $b): int {
  return $a + $b;
}
echo add(5, 3);
?>

php.title: Fix Closure Binding
php.desc: The closure binding scope is wrong.
php.bug:
<?php
class A {
  private $x = 42;
  function getClosure() {
    return function() { return $this->x; };
  }
}
echo (new A())->getClosure()();
?>
php.solution:
<?php
class A {
  private $x = 42;
  function getClosure() {
    return function() { return $this->x; }->bindTo($this);
  }
}
echo (new A())->getClosure()();
?>

php.title: Fix Generator Usage
php.desc: The generator is not properly yielded.
php.bug:
<?php
function gen() {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
  return 3;
}
$g = gen();
foreach ($g as $v) { echo $v; }
echo $g->getReturn();
?>
php.solution:
<?php
function gen() {
  yield 1;

bash.desc: The IFS change affects the entire script.
bash.bug:
#!/bin/bash
data="a,b,c"
OLDIFS=$IFS
IFS=','
for field in $data; do
  echo $field
done
IFS=$OLDIFS
echo "Done"
bash.solution:
#!/bin/bash
data="a,b,c"
while IFS=',' read -ra fields; do
  for field in "${fields[@]}"; do
    echo "$field"
  done
done <<< "$data"
echo "Done"

react.name: React
react.what: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces using a component-based architecture with a virtual DOM for efficient rendering. It enforces a unidirectional data flow and allows developers to compose complex UIs from small, reusable pieces.
react.usedFor: Building single-page applications, complex interactive UIs, mobile apps via React Native, and server-rendered applications through frameworks like Next.js.
react.creator: Jordan Walke, a software engineer at Meta (Facebook). First deployed on Facebook's newsfeed in 2011 and open-sourced at JSConf US in May 2013.

vue.name: Vue
vue.what: Vue is a progressive JavaScript framework for building user interfaces with a reactive, declarative approach. It features a gentle learning curve, a component-based architecture, and a reactive data system that automatically tracks dependencies.
vue.usedFor: Building SPAs, interactive web interfaces, and progressively enhancing existing pages. Vue scales from a simple library to a full-featured framework with Vue Router and Pinia.
vue.creator: Evan You, a former Google engineer who worked on AngularJS. First released in February 2014, with the goal of extracting the best parts of Angular in a more lightweight package.

angular.name: Angular
angular.what: Angular is a comprehensive TypeScript-based web application framework that provides a complete solution for building client-side apps. It includes a powerful template system, dependency injection, routing, forms handling, and HTTP client out of the box.
angular.usedFor: Building large-scale enterprise applications, SPAs, and progressive web apps. Angular's all-in-one approach is popular in corporate environments requiring structured development processes.
angular.creator: Misko Hevery and the Angular team at Google. Originally released as AngularJS in 2010, then completely rewritten as Angular 2+ in 2016.

dk.name: Docker
dk.what: Docker is a containerization platform that packages applications and their dependencies into lightweight, portable containers. Containers run consistently across any environment, eliminating "it works on my machine" problems.
dk.usedFor: Application deployment, microservices architecture, CI/CD pipelines, development environment standardization, and scaling applications across cloud providers.
dk.creator: Solomon Hykes, who started Docker as an internal project at dotCloud (a PaaS company) in 2013. It was open-sourced in March 2013.
dk.code:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# Build: docker build -t myapp .
# Run:   docker run -p 3000:3000 myapp

node.name: Node.js
node.what: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine that allows JavaScript to run on the server. It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model that makes it lightweight and efficient for data-intensive applications.
node.usedFor: Building web servers, REST APIs, real-time applications (chat, gaming), CLI tools, microservices, and back-end services. Node.js has the largest ecosystem of open-source packages (npm).
node.creator: Ryan Dahl, who created Node.js in 2009. Originally sponsored by Joyent, it is now maintained by the OpenJS Foundation under the Node.js Foundation.

express.name: Express
express.what: Express is a minimal and flexible Node.js web application framework that provides a robust set of features for building web and mobile applications. It is the de facto standard server framework for Node.js.
express.usedFor: Building web servers, REST APIs, middleware-based request handling, and as the foundation for many Node.js frameworks (Next.js, NestJS, etc.).
express.creator: TJ Holowaychuk, first released in 2010. Initially created as a side project, it quickly became the most popular Node.js framework. Now maintained by the Node.js Foundation.

next.name: Next.js
next.what: Next.js is a React framework that provides server-side rendering, static site generation, file-based routing, API routes, and built-in optimizations. It abstracts away the complex tooling so developers can focus on building features.
next.usedFor: Building production-grade React applications with SSR, SSG, ISR, and full-stack capabilities. Ideal for content sites, e-commerce, dashboards, and any app needing SEO and performance.
next.creator: Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel (formerly ZEIT). First released in October 2016 as an open-source React framework.

svelte.name: Svelte
svelte.what: Svelte is a radical new approach to building user interfaces — it shifts the work from the browser to the compile step. Instead of using a virtual DOM, Svelte compiles components into highly efficient imperative code that directly manipulates the DOM.
svelte.usedFor: Building fast, reactive web applications with less code. Svelte is great for SPAs, interactive widgets, and tiny bundle-sized apps. Its compile-time approach eliminates the need for a framework runtime.
svelte.creator: Rich Harris, a graphics editor at The New York Times. First released in November 2016 as an open-source compiler.
svelte.code:
<script>
  let count = 0;
  function increment() {
    count += 1;
  }
</script>

<button on:click={increment}>
  Clicked {count} times
</button>

<style>
  button { color: #FF3E00; }
</style>

tailwind.name: Tailwind CSS
tailwind.what: Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework that provides low-level, composable utility classes for building custom designs directly in your markup. Instead of pre-built components, it gives you building blocks to create any design.
tailwind.usedFor: Rapidly building modern, responsive user interfaces with consistent design systems. Tailwind is framework-agnostic and works with React, Vue, Angular, and plain HTML projects.
tailwind.creator: Adam Wathan, first released in November 2017. Inspired by the utility-first approach from projects like Tachyons and Functional CSS.
tailwind.code: Hover me

redis.name: Redis
redis.what: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an open-source, in-memory data structure store that can be used as a database, cache, and message broker. It supports data structures like strings, hashes, lists, sets, and sorted sets with range queries.
redis.usedFor: Caching, session management, real-time analytics, message queues, rate limiting, and as a primary database for high-throughput applications that need sub-millisecond response times.
redis.creator: Salvatore Sanfilippo (known as antirez), first released in 2009. Sponsored by Redis Labs (now Redis Inc.) since 2015.

nuxt.name: Nuxt
nuxt.what: Nuxt is a Vue.js framework that provides server-side rendering, static site generation, file-based routing, auto-imports, and a modular architecture through its module system. It bridges the gap between Vue and production-grade applications.
nuxt.usedFor: Building universal Vue applications with SSR and SSG, SEO-friendly websites, dashboards, and full-stack applications with built-in server routes and middleware.
nuxt.creator: Sebastien Chopin, first released in October 2016. Nuxt 3, released in 2022, was rewritten from the ground up using Vue 3, Vite, and Nitro.
nuxt.code: // app.vue — Nuxt 3

sveltekit.name: SvelteKit
sveltekit.what: SvelteKit is a framework for building Svelte applications with server-side rendering, file-based routing, API endpoints, form actions, and deployment adapters. It is the official successor to Sapper.
sveltekit.usedFor: Building full-stack Svelte applications with SSR, SSG, and server-side logic. SvelteKit is ideal for production-grade apps that need SEO, fast load times, and seamless data fetching.
sveltekit.creator: Rich Harris, the creator of Svelte, at Vercel. First released in public beta in March 2021, with a stable 1.0 release in December 2022.
sveltekit.code:
// src/routes/+page.svelte

Hello, SvelteKit!

remix.name: Remix
remix.what: Remix is a full-stack web framework built on top of React Router that embraces the web platform fundamentals — HTML forms, HTTP methods, and progressive enhancement. It treats the server as a first-class citizen.
remix.usedFor: Building full-stack React applications with server-side rendering, form handling, nested routes, and progressive enhancement. Remix is designed for the modern web with a focus on user experience.
remix.creator: Ryan Florence and Michael Jackson (creators of React Router). First released in public beta in 2021, acquired by Shopify in 2022, and open-sourced in 2023.

vite.name: Vite
vite.what: Vite (French for "quick") is a modern build tool that leverages native ES modules for instant server start and fast Hot Module Replacement. It uses Rollup for production builds with pre-configured optimizations.
vite.usedFor: As a build tool and dev server for JavaScript/TypeScript projects. Vite supports React, Vue, Svelte, vanilla JS, and many other frameworks through plugins.
vite.creator: Evan You, the creator of Vue.js. First released in April 2020 as a faster alternative to webpack for Vue projects, later expanded to support all frameworks.

webpack.name: Webpack
webpack.what: Webpack is a static module bundler that takes modules with dependencies and generates static assets representing those modules. It supports loaders and plugins for transforming and optimizing assets.
webpack.usedFor: Bundling JavaScript applications with dependency management, code splitting, asset processing (CSS, images, fonts), and build optimization for production deployments.
webpack.creator: Tobias Koppers, first released in March 2012. Webpack became the dominant bundler in the React ecosystem and is maintained by the webpack contributors and OpenJS Foundation.

graphql.name: GraphQL
graphql.what: GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a runtime for executing those queries with your existing data. Clients request exactly the data they need, eliminating over-fetching and under-fetching common in REST APIs.
graphql.usedFor: Building flexible, efficient APIs where clients control the response shape. Popular for complex data requirements, mobile APIs, and modern web applications needing precise data fetching.
graphql.creator: Lee Byron and others at Meta (Facebook). Internally developed since 2012, open-sourced in 2015. Now governed by the GraphQL Foundation under the Linux Foundation.

prisma.name: Prisma
prisma.what: Prisma is a next-generation ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) for Node.js and TypeScript that provides a type-safe database client, auto-generated queries, and a declarative data modeling language.
prisma.usedFor: Database access in Node.js/TypeScript applications — querying, migrating, and seeding databases. Prisma supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and MongoDB.
prisma.creator: Johannes Schickling and Nikolas Burk, first released in 2016. Originally a GraphQL database tool, it evolved into a general-purpose ORM. Backed by Prisma Data Platform.

rnative.name: React Native
rnative.what: React Native is a framework for building native mobile applications using JavaScript and React. It compiles to native platform code, giving apps the look, feel, and performance of truly native apps.
rnative.usedFor: Building cross-platform iOS and Android apps with a single React codebase. Popular for mobile apps that need native performance without writing platform-specific code.
rnative.creator: Meta (Facebook). First released as an open-source project on GitHub in 2015. Built on the same principles as React but targeting mobile platforms instead of the web.

flutter.name: Flutter
flutter.what: Flutter is an open-source UI toolkit for building natively compiled applications for mobile, web, and desktop from a single Dart codebase. It uses the Skia graphics engine to render its own widgets, bypassing platform UI components.
flutter.usedFor: Building cross-platform apps for iOS, Android, web, Windows, macOS, and Linux with a single codebase. Popular for MVPs, design-centric apps, and products needing consistent branding.
flutter.creator: Google, first announced in 2015 at the Dart Developer Summit. The first stable version was released in December 2018.

cypress.name: Cypress
cypress.what: Cypress is a developer-friendly end-to-end testing framework built for the modern web. It runs tests inside the browser, providing real-time reloading, time-travel debugging, and automatic waiting.
cypress.usedFor: End-to-end testing, integration testing, and component testing for web applications. Cypress excels at debugging with its interactive test runner and detailed error messages.
cypress.creator: Brian Mann, first released in 2016. Cypress was built from the ground up to solve the pain points developers faced with traditional Selenium-based testing.

playwright.name: Playwright
playwright.what: Playwright is a cross-browser automation framework that enables reliable end-to-end testing across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with a single API. It auto-waits for elements and generates tests via codegen.
playwright.usedFor: Cross-browser testing, web scraping, automation, and performance testing. Playwright supports modern web features like network interception, mobile emulation, and parallel execution.
playwright.creator: Microsoft, first released in January 2019. Built by the same team that created Puppeteer at Google, bringing cross-browser support and improved reliability.

k8s.name: Kubernetes
k8s.what: Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform that automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It groups containers into pods and manages them across clusters of nodes.
k8s.usedFor: Container orchestration in production — deploying, scaling, load-balancing, rolling updates, and self-healing of containerized microservices across cloud and on-premise environments.
k8s.creator: Joe Beda, Brendan Burns, and Craig McLuckie at Google. Based on Google's internal Borg system, first open-sourced in 2014. Now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF).
k8s.code:
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000

terraform.name: Terraform
terraform.what: Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool that lets you define and provision infrastructure using a declarative configuration language called HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language). It manages cloud resources across multiple providers.
terraform.usedFor: Provisioning and managing cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP), version-controlling infrastructure state, automating multi-cloud deployments, and managing infrastructure lifecycles.
terraform.creator: Mitchell Hashimoto at HashiCorp, first released in July 2014. Terraform pioneered the "infrastructure as code" approach and is now an industry standard for cloud provisioning.

bootstrap.name: Bootstrap
bootstrap.what: Bootstrap is the world's most popular front-end component library, providing a responsive grid system, pre-built UI components, and utility classes. It uses a mobile-first approach with a 12-column grid, five responsive breakpoints, and Sass variables for customization. Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery dependency and uses vanilla JavaScript for interactive components.
bootstrap.usedFor: Building responsive websites quickly, prototyping interfaces, creating consistent UI across browsers, and developing admin dashboards. Bootstrap is ideal for projects that need a solid, battle-tested design system out of the box.
bootstrap.creator: Mark Otto and Jacob Thornton at Twitter. Originally released in August 2011 as an internal tool, it was open-sourced and became the most starred project on GitHub.
bootstrap.code:
Bootstrap Card

Built with utility classes and components.

Learn More

django.name: Django
django.what: Django is a high-level Python web framework that encourages rapid development with a clean, pragmatic design. It follows the "batteries-included" philosophy, providing an ORM, admin panel, authentication system, forms, templates, and security features out of the box. Django follows the MTV (Model-Template-View) architectural pattern and emphasizes DRY principles.
django.usedFor: Building database-driven web applications, content management systems, REST APIs (with DRF), e-commerce platforms, and data-driven websites. Django is popular for its security features and rapid development capabilities.
django.creator: Adrian Holovaty and Simon Willison at the Lawrence Journal-World newspaper. First released in 2005 and named after the jazz guitarist Django Reinhardt. Now maintained by the Django Software Foundation.
django.code:
# Install: pip install django # Create: django-admin startproject mysite # views.py from django.http import HttpResponse def home(request): return HttpResponse("

Hello, Django!

") # urls.py from django.urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path("", views.home, name="home"), ] # Run: python manage.py runserver

flask.name: Flask
flask.what: Flask is a lightweight Python web microframework that provides the essentials for building web applications. It is minimal, flexible, and unopinionated — you choose your tools (ORM, template engine, etc.). Flask is built on Werkzeug (WSGI toolkit) and Jinja2 (template engine), making it ideal for small to medium projects, APIs, and microservices.
flask.usedFor: Building REST APIs, microservices, web application prototypes, and small to medium web applications. Flask is popular for its simplicity, flexibility, and extensive ecosystem of extensions.
flask.creator: Armin Ronacher, first released on April 1, 2010 as an April Fools joke that became a serious project. Part of the Pocoo team, now maintained by the Pallets project.

fastapi.name: FastAPI
fastapi.what: FastAPI is a modern, high-performance Python web framework for building APIs with Python 3.8+ based on standard Python type hints. It automatically generates OpenAPI (Swagger) documentation, provides async/await support, and includes a powerful dependency injection system. FastAPI is one of the fastest Python frameworks, rivaling Node.js and Go in performance.
fastapi.usedFor: Building REST APIs, microservices, real-time applications with WebSocket support, and high-performance web services. FastAPI excels in projects requiring automatic API documentation, request validation, and async performance.
fastapi.creator: Sebastián Ramírez (tiangolo), first released in 2018. Built on Starlette (web toolkit) and Pydantic (data validation). FastAPI has rapidly grown to become one of the most popular Python web frameworks.

spring.name: Spring
spring.what: Spring is a comprehensive Java framework for building enterprise applications. Spring Boot simplifies development with auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter dependencies. Key modules include Spring Core (DI/IoC), Spring MVC (web), Spring Data (databases), Spring Security (auth), and Spring Cloud (microservices).
spring.usedFor: Building enterprise Java applications, REST APIs, microservices, batch processing, and cloud-native applications. Spring Boot is the de facto standard for Java web development in enterprise environments.
spring.creator: Rod Johnson, first released in 2003 as a lighter alternative to Enterprise JavaBeans. Spring Boot was later created by Phil Webb and the Pivotal team in 2014 to simplify Spring configuration. Now maintained by VMware.

rails.name: Ruby on Rails
rails.what: Ruby on Rails (Rails) is a full-stack web application framework written in Ruby that follows the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern. It emphasizes convention over configuration, DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles, and rapid development. Rails includes everything needed to build modern web applications: an ORM (ActiveRecord), routing, templating, testing framework, asset pipeline, WebSocket support (ActionCable), background jobs (ActiveJob), and more. Rails has a strong ecosystem of gems and follows a 'batteries-included' philosophy.
rails.usedFor: Building database-backed web applications, RESTful APIs, SaaS platforms, e-commerce systems, content management systems, social networks, and prototypes. Rails is particularly popular for startups and MVPs due to its rapid development capabilities and strong conventions that reduce decision fatigue.
rails.creator: David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) extracted Rails from the Basecamp project in 2004. Rails 1.0 was released in 2005. The framework has gone through major versions (7.x, 8.x) with Hotwire, import maps, and modern JavaScript integration. Rails is maintained by the Rails Core team and a large open-source community.
rails.code:
# Install: gem install rails
# Create: rails new myapp
# Server: rails server

# app/controllers/posts_controller.rb
class PostsController < ApplicationController
  def index
    @posts = Post.all
  end

  def show
    @post = Post.find(params[:id])
  end

  def create
    @post = Post.new(post_params)
    if @post.save
      redirect_to @post
    else
      render :new
    end
  end

  private

  def post_params
    params.require(:post).permit(:title, :body)
  end
end

# app/models/post.rb
class Post < ApplicationRecord
  validates :title, presence: true
  has_many :comments, dependent: :destroy
end

What is a Compiler?.exp:
A compiler is a program that translates source code written in one language into another language — typically from a high-level language (like Python or JavaScript) into low-level machine code, bytecode, or another high-level language.

Think of a compiler as a translator between you (the programmer) and the computer. You write code in a human-readable language; the compiler converts it into instructions the computer can execute.

Why do we need compilers?

  • Computers only understand machine code (1s and 0s)
  • Writing machine code is impractical for humans
  • Compilers let us write in readable languages and still run on hardware
  • Compilers can optimize code to run faster
  • Compilers can catch errors before the program runs

Compilers vs Interpreters:

  • Compiler: Translates all code at once, produces an executable file (C, Go, Rust, Zig)
  • Interpreter: Executes code line by line (Python, JavaScript, Ruby)
  • JIT (Just-In-Time): Compiles code at runtime for speed (Java JVM, V8 for JavaScript)

Try this: Click "Pipeline ▶" in the Compiler mode below the editor to see how code gets tokenized and parsed step by step.

Lexical Analysis.exp:
Tokenization (also called lexical analysis or lexing) is the first stage of compilation. It breaks source code into meaningful chunks called tokens.

A token is the smallest unit of meaning in a programming language — keywords, identifiers, operators, numbers, strings, punctuation, etc.

Examples of tokens:

  • let — keyword token
  • myVariable — identifier token
  • = — operator token
  • 42 — number token
  • "hello" — string token
  • ; — punctuation token
  • // comment — comment token

How tokenizers work:

  1. Read source code character by character
  2. Group characters into tokens based on patterns
  3. Classify each token (keyword, identifier, number, etc.)
  4. Output a token stream for the parser

Why tokenization matters:

  • Simplifies the parser (works with tokens, not raw characters)
  • Catches basic errors (invalid characters, unterminated strings)
  • Removes whitespace and comments from the parse stream
  • Maps source positions for error reporting

Try this: Write code in the editor and click "Tokenize ▶" to see every token the compiler finds in your code.

Syntax Analysis.exp:
Parsing (syntax analysis) takes the flat token stream from the lexer and builds a tree structure called the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).

An AST represents the grammatical structure of your code as a tree. Each node in the tree represents a construct (variable declaration, function call, expression, etc.) and its children represent the components.

Why an AST?

  • Captures the hierarchy of code (blocks inside functions inside classes)
  • Ignores syntactic sugar (semicolons, parentheses in some cases)
  • Makes it easy to transform or analyze code
  • Enables optimizations and code generation

Common AST node types:

  • Program — the root of every AST
  • FunctionDeclaration — a function definition
  • VariableDeclaration — declaring a variable
  • BinaryExpression — a + b, x > 5
  • CallExpression — calling a function: foo()
  • Block — a group of statements in { }
  • ControlFlow — if, for, while

Parsing strategies:

  • Recursive Descent: Most common for hand-written parsers. One function per grammar rule.
  • LL/LR Parsers: Generated from grammar definition. Used in production compilers (GCC, Clang).
  • Operator Precedence: Specific technique for parsing expressions with operator precedence.

Try this: Click "AST ▶" to see the tree structure the compiler builds from your code.

Generating Output.exp:
Code generation is the final stage of the compiler pipeline. It walks the AST and produces output code in the target language.

For most compilers, the output is machine code or bytecode. In this Compiler Explorer, you can see how the same code would be compiled to different output representations:

  • JavaScript: Same as input (JS is interpreted)
  • Machine code view: Conceptual translation to low-level instructions
  • Structural output: What the compiler "sees" in your code

What code generators do:

  1. Walk the AST (depth-first or breadth-first)
  2. For each node type, emit appropriate output code
  3. Track context (scope, registers, variable locations)
  4. Optimize the output (peephole optimization, register allocation)

Example walk: For let x = 5 + 3

  1. Visit Program node → start new line
  2. Visit VariableDeclaration → emit let x =
  3. Visit BinaryExpression → emit 5 + 3
  4. Visit number "5" → emit 5
  5. Visit operator "+" → emit +
  6. Visit number "3" → emit 3
  7. Finish line → emit ;

Real compiler optimizations:

  • Constant folding: 5 + 3 → 8 (evaluated at compile time)
  • Dead code elimination: Remove code that never runs
  • Inlining: Replace function calls with the function body
  • Loop unrolling: Duplicate loop body for performance

All Languages Supported.exp:
This Compiler Explorer analyzes code from all 15+ languages in Kodex's Lab! The tokenizer and AST builder adapt to each language's syntax.

How it works across languages:

  • Comment styles: // (JS/TS/C/C++/etc.), # (Python/Docker), -- (SQL)
  • String delimiters: ", ', backticks, """ (Python/Kotlin)
  • Block structure: { } for most languages, indentation for Python
  • Keywords: Per-language keyword sets for accurate token classification
  • Operators: Universal operators plus language-specific ones (-> in Go/C, => in JS)

Switch languages and click Pipeline to see!

The tokenizer recognizes language-specific syntax including:

  • Python: def, class:, indentation-based blocks
  • Go: func, defer, go routines
  • Rust: fn, match, impl, trait
  • SQL: Case-insensitive keywords, SELECT, FROM, JOIN
  • Docker: FROM, RUN, CMD
  • Git: Commands and flags
  • MongoDB: Query operators $match, $group

Type Checking & Scope.exp:
Semantic analysis is the compiler stage that checks whether code makes logical sense — beyond just syntax.

While parsing checks structure (grammar), semantic analysis checks meaning. This is where the compiler catches real bugs.

What semantic analysis checks:

  • Type checking: Are operands the right types? "hello" - 5 is syntactically valid but semantically wrong in most languages.
  • Scope resolution: Does each variable reference point to a valid declaration?
  • Name binding: Are functions, types, and variables used before declaration (where required)?
  • Type inference: Can the compiler deduce types without explicit annotations?

Type systems spectrum:

  • Dynamic: Types checked at runtime (Python, JavaScript) — flexible but error-prone
  • Static: Types checked at compile time (C, Go, Rust) — catches errors early
  • Gradual: Mix of both (TypeScript, Python with type hints)
  • Strong: No implicit type coercion (Python, Rust)
  • Weak: Implicit coercion allowed (C, JavaScript)

Semantic errors vs syntax errors:

  • Syntax error: let 5x = 3; — the grammar doesn't allow this
  • Semantic error: let x: number = "hello"; — grammatically valid, but type mismatch

Making Code Faster.exp:
Compiler optimization transforms code to run faster, use less memory, or consume less power — without changing its meaning.

Most optimizations are conservative: the compiler only applies them when it's sure the program's behavior won't change.

Categories of optimization:

  • Constant folding: x = 5 + 3 → x = 8 (evaluate at compile time)
  • Constant propagation: If x = 5, replace all uses of x with 5
  • Dead code elimination: Remove branches that never execute or variables never read
  • Loop unrolling: Duplicate loop body to reduce overhead of the loop control
  • Function inlining: Replace function call with the function body itself
  • Strength reduction: Replace expensive ops with cheaper ones (e.g., x * 2 → x << 1)
  • Common subexpression elimination: Compute a value once and reuse it

Optimization levels in GCC/Clang:

  • -O0: No optimization (fastest compile, slowest code)
  • -O1: Basic optimizations (good balance)
  • -O2: More aggressive (recommended for release builds)
  • -O3: Very aggressive (may increase code size)
  • -Os: Optimize for size (embedded systems)

From AST to Machine Code.exp:
Between the high-level AST and the low-level machine code, most compilers use one or more intermediate representations (IRs).

IRs bridge the gap between the source language and the target hardware, making the compiler easier to port to new architectures.

Common IRs:

  • Three-Address Code (TAC): Simple instruction format: t1 = a + b
  • Static Single Assignment (SSA): Each variable assigned exactly once — enables powerful optimizations (used by LLVM, GCC)
  • LLVM IR: A low-level, typed IR used by Clang, rustc, and many others
  • Bytecode: Portable IR for virtual machines (JVM bytecode, Python bytecode, WASM)
  • C as IR: Some compilers output C code and let the C compiler handle machine code generation

Why multi-level IRs?

  • Frontend (language-specific) → high-level IR → mid-level IR → low-level IR → machine code
  • Each level enables different optimizations
  • New language backends only need to generate IR, not full machine code

LLVM's architecture: The most popular compiler infrastructure uses this exact pattern. Language frontends (Clang for C/C++, rustc for Rust) all emit LLVM IR, which LLVM optimizes and compiles to native code.

branch.title: Welcome to Branching!
branch.text: Branches let you work on features independently. The graph shows your commit history on main.

branch.title: Create a Branch
branch.text: Run git branch feature to create a new branch called "feature". It points to your current commit.

branch.title: Switch Branches
branch.text: Now run git checkout feature to switch to your new branch. See how HEAD moves?

branch.title: Commit on Feature
branch.text: Make a commit on feature: git commit -m "Add login page". Notice the graph forks.

branch.title: Switch Back
branch.text: Run git checkout main to go back to main. HEAD moves back to main.

branch.title: Another Main Commit
branch.text: Commit on main too: git commit -m "Update README". The branches now diverge.

branch.title: Done!
branch.text: You mastered branching! Try other scenarios to learn merge, rebase, squash, and cherry-pick.

merge.title: Welcome to Merge!
merge.text: Merging combines work from different branches. Here feature has commits ahead of main.

merge.title: Check Main
merge.text: First, ensure you're on main: git checkout main.

merge.title: Merge Feature
merge.text: Now merge feature into main: git merge feature. A merge commit appears!

merge.title: Done!
merge.text: You merged! The graph now shows the combined history. Tip: merge commits have two parents.

rebase.title: Welcome to Rebase!
rebase.text: Rebase rewrites history by moving your branch commits on top of another branch. feature is behind main.

rebase.title: Checkout Feature
rebase.text: Switch to feature branch: git checkout feature.

rebase.title: Rebase onto Main
rebase.text: Run git rebase main to move feature commits on top of main. The graph realigns!

rebase.title: Done!
rebase.text: Feature commits now sit on top of main. Note: rebase rewrites commit hashes — careful with shared branches!

squash.title: Welcome to Squash!
squash.text: Squashing combines multiple messy commits into one. feature has several tiny commits.

squash.title: Squash Feature
squash.text: Run git merge --squash feature from main. This collects all feature commits into staged changes.

squash.title: Commit the Squash
squash.text: Now commit to finalize: git commit -m "Add feature (squashed)". One clean commit!

squash.title: Done!
squash.text: All those messy WIP commits are now one clean commit on main. Much cleaner!

cherrypick.title: Welcome to Cherry-Pick!
cherrypick.text: Cherry-pick lets you grab specific commits from another branch. Only one commit gets applied.

cherrypick.title: Find a Commit
cherrypick.text: Look at the graph. The feature branch has commits like "Fix security bug". Pick its ID from the graph!

cherrypick.title: Cherry-Pick It
cherrypick.text: Run git cherry-pick p5q6r7 to grab the "Fix security bug" commit.

cherrypick.title: Done!
cherrypick.text: Only the security fix landed on main, without the rest of the feature branch.

freeplay.title: Welcome to Freeplay!
freeplay.text: This is a sandbox. Start by typing git init in the terminal below to create a fresh repository.

freeplay.title: Make a Commit
freeplay.text: Great! Now make your first commit: git commit -m "Initial commit".

freeplay.title: Create a Branch
freeplay.text: Create a branch: git branch feature. See the new lane appear!

freeplay.title: Commit on Feature
freeplay.text: Commit on feature: git commit -m "Add feature work".

freeplay.title: Back to Main
freeplay.text: Go back to main: git checkout main.

freeplay.title: Merge It
freeplay.text: Merge your feature: git merge feature. A merge commit with two parents appears!

freeplay.title: Done!
freeplay.text: You just did a full workflow: init → commit → branch → checkout → commit → merge. Now experiment freely!

branch.name: Branching
branch.desc: Practice creating and switching branches. Type: git branch feature, git checkout feature, git commit -m "msg"

merge.name: Merge
merge.desc: Practice merging branches. A feature branch is ready. Type: git checkout main, then git merge feature

rebase.name: Rebase
rebase.desc: Practice rebasing. Feature branch is behind main. Type: git checkout feature, then git rebase main

squash.name: Squash
squash.desc: Practice squashing commits. Feature has messy commits. Try: git merge --squash feature from main, or git rebase -i

cherrypick.name: Cherry-Pick
cherrypick.desc: Practice cherry-picking specific commits. Type: git checkout main, then git cherry-pick <commit-id>

freeplay.name: Freeplay
freeplay.desc: Sandbox mode. Type git init to start, then branch, commit, merge, rebase — experiment freely!

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: Welcome to Schema Designer
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
▦

Schema Designer Tutorial

Learn to visually design database schemas — add tables, define columns, set constraints, create relationships, and generate production-ready SQL.

Tables & ColumnsConstraints (PK, NN, UQ)Foreign KeysIndexesSQL GenerationERD View

10 steps · ~5 minutes

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: Tables
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Tables store your data in rows and columns

Click "+ Table" in the toolbar to add a table. Each table starts with two default columns (id and name). You can drag tables around the canvas to arrange them. Click the name input to rename — use lowercase plural nouns like users, orders, products.

Generated SQL:

CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: Columns & Data Types
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Define the structure of your data

Each column needs a name and a type. Use the "col name" field and type dropdown in each table row. Available types:

INTSERIALBIGINTVARCHAR(255)TEXTBOOLEANDATETIMESTAMPDECIMALUUIDJSONBFLOAT

Each type maps to the appropriate dialect-specific type when you switch dialects.

CREATE TABLE products (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL NOT NULL,
    in_stock BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: Constraints
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Enforce data integrity

Toggle constraints on any column using the badges and checkbox in each row:

PKPrimary Key — uniquely identifies each row
NNNOT NULL — column must have a value
UQUNIQUE — no duplicate values allowed
DFDEFAULT — sets a fallback value if none is provided
CREATE TABLE employees (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    department VARCHAR(100) DEFAULT 'engineering'
);

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: Foreign Keys
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Link tables together

A foreign key creates a relationship between two tables. To create one:

  1. Click the "~>" handle on the source column
  2. Then click a column in the target table
  3. A colored bezier curve appears showing the relationship

Cardinality labels (* and 1) show one-to-many relationships. Click an existing FK badge to remove it.

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    total DECIMAL,
    status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'pending'
);

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: Indexes
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Speed up your queries

Indexes make database queries faster by allowing quick lookups on specific columns. To add one:

  1. Click "+ Index" below a table
  2. Name your index (e.g., idx_users_email)
  3. Select which columns to include
  4. Toggle UNIQUE if the index should enforce uniqueness
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: ERD View
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Visualize relationships

The ERD (Entity-Relationship Diagram) view shows a simplified, read-only visualization of your schema:

  • Compact table cards with PK and FK badges
  • Constraint flags: NN, UQ, DF
  • Dashed lines represent relationships
  • Click a row to create or remove FK links (same click-to-link flow)
  • Drag tables to reposition

Switch between Design and ERD using the tabs at the top of the schema designer.

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: SQL Generation
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Generate production-ready DDL

The SQL Preview panel at the bottom of the schema designer auto-generates DDL as you design, with a 500ms debounce.

Switch dialects using the dropdown to see how the same schema translates:

PostgreSQLMySQLSQLite

Use Copy to copy to clipboard or Download to save as a .sql file.

-- PostgreSQL
CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

-- MySQL
CREATE TABLE users (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4;

-- SQLite
CREATE TABLE users (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name TEXT NOT NULL
);

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.title: Import, Export & Versioning
SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:
Save and restore your work

Import SQL

Paste CREATE TABLE statements to parse them into the visual designer. Supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite dialects.

Export JSON / SQL

Download your schema as a JSON file (for re-import) or as a SQL file (for direct use).

Undo / Redo

Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y for 50-deep undo/redo stack. Never lose your changes.

Version History

Save named snapshots of your schema to localStorage. Restore or delete them anytime.

SCHEMA_TUT_STEPS.body:

You've Completed the Tutorial!

You now know how to use every feature of the Schema Designer. Click the button below to open the practice workspace and start designing your own schemas!

Tip: You can replay this tutorial anytime by clicking the Tutorial button in the schema toolbar.

ERROR_PATTERNS.title: Syntax Error
ERROR_PATTERNS.tip:
A syntax error means the parser couldn't understand your code. Common causes:
- Missing bracket, parenthesis, or curly brace
- Missing comma between elements
- Using a keyword as a variable name

**Quick fix:** Look at the line number in the error and check for unbalanced `{`, `(`, `[`, or missing `,`.

ERROR_PATTERNS.title: Reference Error
ERROR_PATTERNS.tip:
This means you're trying to use a variable or function that doesn't exist yet.

Common causes:
- **Typo:** Did you spell it the same everywhere? JavaScript is case-sensitive!
- **Not declared:** Did you use `let`, `const`, or `var` to declare it?
- **Out of scope:** Is the variable accessible from where you're trying to use it?

re.source: TypeError|is not a function|Cannot read property

ERROR_PATTERNS.title: Type Error
ERROR_PATTERNS.tip:
TypeError means a value is not the type you expected.

Common causes:
- **undefined value:** `arr[0]` might be `undefined`, then calling `.name` on it fails
- **Wrong type:** `"hello" - 5` doesn't work (but `"hello" + 5` does — string concatenation!)
- **Not a function:** `arr.length()` is wrong — `length` is a property, not a method

ERROR_PATTERNS.title: Range Error
ERROR_PATTERNS.tip:
RangeError means a value is outside the allowed range.

Common causes:
- **Infinite recursion:** Your function calls itself without reaching a base case
- **Array size:** Trying to create an array with a negative length
- **Stack overflow:** Too many nested function calls

ERROR_PATTERNS.title: Execution Error
ERROR_PATTERNS.tip:
Your code ran into an error during execution. Let's debug it step by step:
1. Read the error message carefully — it tells you the line number
2. Check the line it points to and the lines just before it
3. Add `console.log()` to print values and see where things go wrong
